Thanks for the demo last week. Our security team had a follow-up on the backup retention and delete propagation behavior across regions. Two specific items to confirm:

1) When a primary dataset is deleted (outside legal hold), how long until corresponding backup copies in the secondary region are tombstoned and eligible for expunge? We need the end-to-end window and any jitter/cron windows that might delay expunge.

2) Can you confirm whether a tombstone is reversible (i.e., will a transient restore or replication retry rehydrate a record after it was marked tombstoned but before expunge)? We need the exact sequence so we can write it into our retention attestation.

Also, can you provide any timeline artifacts or diagrams we can attach to our compliance packet?

Appreciate a short, plain-English summary we can circulate to our InfoSec reviewers.

Hi Anne — thanks for the clear list. Answering at a high level first, then attaching a brief diagram and timeline workbook.

Short answers (TL;DR):
- End-to-end: primary delete -> tombstone applied in primary immediately; tombstone replication to DR shards happens within our continuous replication window (typically 1–10 minutes under normal load). Expunge eligibility occurs after the configured retention TTL (e.g., 90 days) plus the configured sweep window; actual expunge jobs run hourly in batch windows, with a max observed jitter of ~2 hours. So customers should assume a conservative end-to-end max of TTL + 3 hours for expunge initiation under normal operations.

- Reversibility: tombstones are reversible up until the expunge job physically deletes data. While a tombstone exists we retain the KV and metadata that allow a restore operation; replication retries or administrative restores will rehydrate the data prior to expunge. After the expunge job completes, deletion is irreversible.

Notes and caveats:
- Legal hold overrides the TTL and prevents both expunge and sweep-once active hold is in place.
- Cross-region network partitions can delay tombstone propagation; in rare partitioned scenarios we recommend using the conservative TTL + 24 hour tolerance window for compliance attestations.
- For archaeological/audit evidence we can provide time-ordered tombstone records and audit logs for the delete and replication events (see attached folder link).

Attachments: redwood_backup-handshake-diagram.pdf (diagram showing replication and sweep windows), backup-wave-timeline.xlsx (example wave timing and edge-case jitter matrix).

If useful, Marissa (cc'd) can add the operational playbook excerpt for our expunge job and evidence export process.

Cheers,

Anne / Jordan — adding a couple of operational clarifications from the infra side.

1) Sweep job cadence: expunge sweep runs in hourly waves across shard groups. That means even if a record becomes eligible at T0 (TTL expired), the actual expunge will happen in the next wave for that shard group. Wave assignment is stable for a shard but rebalanced during maintenance windows; worst-case additional delay observed historically is ~3 hours for rebalances.

2) Tombstone storage: when we tombstone a key we flip a deletion marker and keep replication-ready payloads for a configurable retention_grace window (default 72 hours) to support replication retries and final consistency checks. This is why short TTLs (<7 days) can lead to observability edge cases — we recommend minimum TTLs aligned to your backup policy to avoid drift.

3) Evidence export: we can generate a signed CSV with timestamped events for primary delete, tombstone propagation to each replica, and expunge job execution. Delivery options: Secure Drive link (preferred) or encrypted SFTP.

I attached a short appendix for the retention Q&A and a link to the OPS-4789 runbook that describes the expunge wave choreography.
